e: Plain English Words this page uses because the court uses them. Nothing here is special to this case. The paperwork How a case moves The motions that can end things Tests the court applies

United States District Court · Southern District of Florida · No. 1:25-cv-20757-JB Doe v. Bonnell A civil lawsuit over an intimate video. It was recorded with consent, and later Bonnell sent it to someone else. Years afterward a third party put it online and it spread. The fight over who’s to blame lit up the political streaming world, which was already divided, and most people took the side they always would have based on the online community they were a part of. In court, almost all of it turns on one date, October 1, 2022, when the federal law Doe is suing under took effect. Filed Feb 18, 2025 Before Becerra, J. · Torres, M.J. Docket 311 entries Status Undecided

Plaintiff The side that sued Stand-in name Jane Doe is the stand-in name courts use when someone is allowed to sue without using their real name. The judge allowed it here the day after she asked, and the law she’s suing under allows for it, so this page doesn’t name her either. Her complaint says that she lives in the Miami area, that she’s a live streamer like Bonnell, and that she was new to political streaming when the two of them first started talking. ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 6, 9–10 · ECF No. 7

Defendant The side that was sued Streamer, known online as Destiny He’s a live streamer and political commentator who goes by Destiny. He was born in Omaha, Nebraska, in 1988. In 2011 he started streaming the video game StarCraft II full time, and he was one of the first people to make a living that way. Around 2016 he moved over to politics, and he’s best known now for long live debates where he argues from the liberal side. He lives in Miami Beach. ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 7–8 · ECF No. 42-1 ¶ 3 · Background: Wikipedia
Notes Record reviewed through October 7, 2026 . Nothing filed after that date is reflected here.
How this was made, and what it leaves out

Built from the complete public docket, 311 entries as of October 7, 2026, as archived by the Free Law Project from PACER. Every characterization here comes from a filing, an exhibit, or a signed order. Every docket number in a citation opens that filing, in the archive it came from. The court’s paperless orders have no document behind them, so those open the docket entry itself. Deposition citations open the transcript at the page cited.

A great deal. The plaintiff’s legal name, several witness identities, three of the four deposition transcripts and many exhibits were never filed publicly. The defendant’s transcript reached the docket in September 2026, redacted. Some of what each side relies on cannot be read by anyone outside the case.

The plaintiff sued under a pseudonym and the court granted it. Non-party witnesses appear here only by the screen names already used in public filings. The explicit material quoted in the record is described, not reproduced.

Not legal advice, not a finding, and not a verdict. Allegations are allegations. No court has resolved the central factual dispute, and the two motions that could have were still pending when this record ends.
The court’s numbered list of everything filed in a case. Entry 42 is the forty-second thing filed.
How a filing is cited: its docket number. A number after a dash, like 42-4, is an attachment to it — usually an exhibit.
The document that starts a lawsuit and sets out what the plaintiff says happened. An amended complaint replaces it.
The defendant’s formal response to the complaint, admitting or denying each allegation.
A written statement signed under penalty of perjury. It counts as evidence without the witness appearing in person.
A document, screenshot or record attached to a filing as proof of something asserted in it.
The word-for-word record of a hearing or a deposition. Cited by page and line, so 55:7 means page 55, line 7.
A formal correction a witness files to their own sworn testimony after reading it back.
Filed with the court but kept off the public record. Both sides and the judge can read it; nobody else can.
A formal request that the court do something. The other side files an opposition; the moving side may then file a reply.
The stage where each side must hand over relevant evidence to the other. It has a deadline, and missing it matters.
Sworn question-and-answer, out of court, recorded by a court reporter. Lawyers for both sides attend; there is no judge.
A court order compelling someone who is not a party to hand over documents or give testimony.
A hearing where witnesses actually testify and are cross-examined, rather than lawyers simply arguing.
An order limiting what either side may do with the material it receives in discovery.
A court order to do something or to stop doing it. A temporary restraining order is the emergency version, and a preliminary injunction lasts while the case goes on. Neither decides who is right.

The emergency version of an injunction, formally a temporary restraining order. A judge can grant one quickly, sometimes before the other side has been heard, to stop harm that cannot wait. It lasts only a short time, usually no more than two weeks, and it does not decide who is right.
A judge who handles pre-trial matters. On some questions they recommend, and the district judge decides.
A short ruling typed straight onto the docket. It has no document behind it, so its citation opens the docket entry instead.
A pause ordered by the court. Whatever is stayed sits on hold until something else is decided first.
What the case is actually about, meaning what happened and who is in the right. A ruling that a court cannot hear a case says nothing about the merits.
Argues the case cannot proceed even if everything alleged is true — usually because the court lacks power to hear it.
Argues the facts are not genuinely in dispute, so the judge can decide without a trial. If facts are disputed, it fails.
Filed before trial to decide what a jury will and will not be allowed to hear.
Destroying or losing evidence you were obliged to keep. The duty starts once you know a lawsuit is coming.
A penalty for misconduct in the litigation itself. They can run from a fine to losing the case outright.
A sanction where the jury is told it may assume the destroyed evidence would have hurt the side that destroyed it.
The rule requiring that filings have a factual basis. A Rule 11 motion says the other side asserted something it could not support.
Whether this court has the power to hear this case at all. A federal court needs a federal claim, which is why one date decides so much here.
Which side has to prove a thing. If they do not, they lose that point, even if the other side proves nothing either.
More likely than not. It is the usual standard of proof in a civil case, and a lower bar than the criminal one.
Whether a law reaches conduct from before it existed. Usually it does not, unless Congress clearly said so.
Repeating what someone said outside court to prove it was true. Generally not allowed, with many exceptions.
Showing a document or screenshot is genuinely what its proponent says it is. The bar is low, but it is not nothing.
Actually tending to prove something. Evidence can be admissible and still carry very little weight.
Where it stands Waiting on the spoliation ruling. Everything under it is stayed until then. Either way If October 2022 If April 2022 If yes If no If yes If no
Should he be ordered to take the video down before the case is decided?
Six weeks after she sued · April 2025

Only about what happens while the case goes on No · denied Apr 4 and Oct 6, 2025 Six weeks after she sued, she asked the judge for an injunction, which is a court order telling someone to do something or to stop doing it. She wanted one right away, before anything in the case had been proven. She wanted him ordered to stop sharing the video, to take down any copies he controlled, and to tell other people in writing to take down theirs. She also wanted him ordered to keep all of his evidence. She asked for an emergency order first, and the judge said no the very next day, on April 4, 2025. Her own lawyer admitted most of the damage had already been done, and the judge said nothing was happening that wasn’t already happening when she sued. The rest of her request got a hearing in June 2025, where both of them testified, and the court turned it down on October 6, 2025. It said she waited five months after the leak to ask, and that this is the kind of harm money can make up for if she wins. None of that decides the case, because it was only ever about what happens while the case goes on. So either way, the case carries on to the questions below. On April 4 the judge also told her lawyers that if they thought he was getting rid of evidence, they needed to file a separate motion about it. They didn’t file one until thirteen months later, and that’s the spoliation motion further down this page.
When did he first send the video?

The send both sides agree happened Apr 9, 2022 · agreed May 8, 2026 The federal law she’s suing under only covers things done on or after October 1, 2022. A law normally isn’t retroactive, meaning it doesn’t reach back to things that happened before it existed. He has always admitted sending the video to one person on Discord, a chat app, to an account called “Rose,” so the fight here was only ever about when. She sued saying it was October 2022. He said it was April 9, 2022, and showed screenshots of the same chat taken from both ends. His end says 4/9/2022. The other end says 10/04/2022, which looks like October 4. But the person behind “Rose” turned out to be a man in the UK, where dates are written day first, so 10/04/2022 means April 10. It was already past midnight in the UK, which is why his end says April 9 and theirs says April 10. Another message in the same chat is dated 14/04/2022, and since there’s no fourteenth month, the dates in that chat have to be day first. In September 2025 the judge called the evidence on the timeline “murky at best,” and let her rewrite her complaint to add two other ways of getting past the date. Those are the two routes in the question at the bottom of this page. Then in May 2026 she agreed it was April 9, 2022. That’s about six months too early, so this send can’t carry a federal claim by itself.

Outcome Then Trial on the merits If the video had first gone out in October 2022, after the law started, that one send would be all she needed. The federal law would cover it, and the court would have jurisdiction, which is its power to hear the case. The question at the bottom of this page, about whether he shared it again later, wouldn’t matter. What would come next is a trial on the merits, meaning a trial about what actually happened and who is in the right. The big fight there would be over consent, since he admits he never asked her.
Should he lose the case for destroying evidence?

The case is here Decided first, and apart from the rest Undecided Spoliation means destroying or losing evidence you were supposed to keep. The plaintiff says he deleted his side of some conversations after he’d been told in writing to keep them. She also says he swore that a log he filed listed everything he ever sent one witness, but his own messages show him sending that witness two links that aren’t on it. So she filed a motion, which is a formal request to the judge, asking for him to be penalized for it. He says nothing was actually lost, and that she filed it too late. Judge Becerra is deciding this first, and everything below it is on hold until she does. The most the plaintiff asked for is a ruling, with no trial, that he is legally responsible, and that’s the yes on this card. If it goes that way, the question below never has to be answered at all. Anything less is a no here, and the case just moves down to that question. That covers the judge siding with the defendant, throwing the motion out for being late, or picking a smaller penalty, like the jury being told it can assume the missing evidence was bad for him.

Outcome Then Decided in her favor without a trial This is the most she asked for. The judge would rule that he is legally responsible without a trial on it, as the penalty for losing evidence he was supposed to keep. The rule she is relying on only allows that if he got rid of it on purpose, so that she couldn’t use it. If it went this way, the argument over what happened would be over, and in her favor. What would be left is how much he owes her. The question under it, about whether he shared the video again after the law started, would never have to be answered.
Did he disclose the video after October 1, 2022?
His two motions to end the case

What the whole case comes down to Stayed until that ruling This is the question the whole case comes down to. The federal law she is suing under took effect on October 1, 2022, and it can’t be used for anything that happened before that. Both sides now agree he sent the video to someone in April 2022, which is about six months too early. So she has to show that he disclosed it, in the law’s sense, at some point after that date. “Disclose” is the law’s own word, and it covers sending something, publishing it, or making it accessible. If she can’t show that, there is no federal claim, and a federal court has no jurisdiction, meaning no power to hear the case at all. She has two different ways of trying to show it, and those are the two routes inside this card. A yes on either one makes this a yes. He has asked the judge twice to end the case on exactly this point, first with a motion to dismiss in September 2025 and then with a motion for summary judgment in January 2026. Both are stayed right now, which means the judge has put them on hold until the spoliation motion above is decided. Who must prove it She does. The burden is on the plaintiff, and she has to meet it by a preponderance of the evidence, which just means more likely than not. A yes on either one is enough or
Could a jury credit an untested declaration?

Undecided This is her first way of getting past that date. She says he sent the video a second time in November 2023, to a witness who goes by “Abbymc” online. That would be thirteen months after the law took effect, so if it happened, it counts. He says it never happened, and points to his own saved logs of what he sent her, where the video doesn’t show up. What she has is two declarations from Abbymc, which are sworn written statements, saying she received it. She also has a message Abbymc sent a friend that same morning. Whether that’s enough is the question this card asks. This is the test Route A has to pass. To credit a statement just means to believe it. A declaration does count as evidence, but Abbymc herself has never been questioned by either side. She never sat for a deposition, which is sworn questioning outside of court. She handed over nothing when she was sent a subpoena, which is a court order to produce documents or testify. And a few days after signing her first declaration she told the defendant she didn’t want to be involved anymore. So the judge has to decide if a reasonable jury could still believe her on paper alone. If it could, the two sides have a real disagreement about a fact, and only a trial can settle that. If it couldn’t, Route A is closed.
Does “make accessible” reach a private link?

Undecided This is her second way, and it doesn’t need a second send at all. The law doesn’t only cover sending or publishing a video. It also covers making it accessible. The copy he sent in April 2022 stayed reachable until he deleted it in November 2024, and he has admitted that under oath. So her argument is that even though the sending happened too early, leaving it reachable went on for about two years after the law took effect, and that this counts as a disclosure all by itself. This is the test Route B has to pass, and it’s about what the words of the law mean, not about what happened. He never posted the video anywhere public himself. He sent it to one person privately, and even her own expert agreed the link was basically impossible to guess. The defendant says that isn’t making something accessible in any real sense, and that she is stretching one message from April 2022 into something that lasts for years so that a newer law can reach it. She says the law says “make accessible,” not “publish,” so it doesn’t have to be public. No court has applied this law to a private link like this before, so whichever way the judge goes, it will be a first. If she wins this one, the federal court keeps the case even if Route A fails.

Outcome Then Trial on the merits If either route works, she has a disclosure after the date, and the federal court has jurisdiction, which is the power to hear the case at all. What comes next is a trial on the merits. That means a trial about what actually happened and who is in the right, instead of about whether this court can hear it. She would go into that trial in a strong position on the main issue, which is consent. He admits he sent the video, and he has testified that he never asked her. He says permission was implied by their earlier exchanges, but the law asks for consent that was actually given.
Neither route · The April 2022 transmission only

Outcome Then Case ends here If neither route passes its test, the only sharing anyone has proven is the one from April 2022. That’s about six months before the law took effect. She used to argue it happened in October 2022, but in May 2026 she agreed that the real date was April 9, 2022. A law normally doesn’t apply retroactively, meaning to things that happened before it existed, so that one send can’t support a federal claim. With no disclosure after the date, there’s nothing left under the federal law. Her other three claims are under Florida law, and they’re only in this court because they grew out of the same facts as the federal one. So when the federal claim goes, the judge will most likely dismiss the Florida claims too, and the case is over in this court. She has asked the judge to keep them anyway, since the case is so close to trial. That wouldn’t be a ruling that he did nothing wrong. It would be a ruling that this court isn’t allowed to decide it. The Florida claims would be dismissed without prejudice, which means she could bring them again in a Florida court.

Read as a whole the pattern is one-sided: the plaintiff has lost most of what she has asked for: on delay, on choosing the wrong procedural vehicle, on asking for a restraint the First Amendment does not permit in a civil case. None of it goes to whether her underlying account is true. The judge who denied her injunction also found her testimony “fully credible.”
The events preceding the case itself. Only events that happened after 10/1/22 can support a federal claim.

She sends him a private message after a debate on a streaming platform. A friendship follows. She sent the first message. Both sides describe what followed the same way, as a friendship where they eventually shared their sex lives with each other, though they disagreed on the implications of that fact. Bonnell Decl. ¶ 5 · ECF No. 42-1

In Miami, consensually. Neither side has ever said otherwise. When the court denied a motion later on, it pointed this out in detail. Neither side says the recording, or what it shows, happened without consent. That matters, because it leaves only the sharing in dispute. ECF No. 142 at 5

Over Discord, to an account he took to be a college student’s. He admits this, and the plaintiff now accepts the date. His declaration puts the transmission at 8:36 p.m. Eastern. The account was actually run by an adult man in the United Kingdom who was using a real woman’s identity. That came out three and a half years later, when the woman herself was deposed. He states he has sent the video to no one since. Bonnell Decl. (Apr 2025) ¶¶ 9–10 · ECF No. 42-1 · Bonnell Decl. (Jan 2026) ¶¶ 2, 3, 5, 7 · ECF No. 213

Oct 1, 2022 15 U.S.C. § 6851 takes effect The statute isn’t retroactive. It covers events that happened after this line and nothing before it, which is why the dates of what he sent decide whether a federal court can hear the case at all.

To a witness known as “Abbymc.” Bonnell has denied it from the start, and it is one of the two ways the federal claim can survive. The witness swears she received the video by Google Drive link and recognized the plaintiff. Her message to a friend that morning is timestamped 10:41 a.m. The defendant’s log puts his only links that day at 2:39 p.m. The plaintiff reads that as a four-hour gap, and his reply never addresses it. At his deposition, though, he said he was not sure which time zone the log uses. If it is universal time, 2:39 p.m. would be 10:39 a.m. in Miami, two minutes before her message. Abbymc Decl. ¶¶ 6–7 · ECF Nos. 49-2, 86-1 · Dep. Tr. 221:3–13

A third party operating as “SoloTinyLeaks” publishes a cache of his private files, including this video, to a forum. Neither party consented. Twenty-nine files went up at once. The forum’s own operator posted that the resulting traffic surge caused a database failure. From there the video spread to several pornography sites, captioned with both parties’ screen names. ECF Nos. 42-8, 52-3

He hires a lawyer who specializes in this, and he and the plaintiff work together on requests to get sites to take the video down. Their messages show him hunting for a DMCA contact, emailing a registrar and passing her a search-removal form while she sends him further URLs. He cites this as proof there was nothing left for an injunction to order him to do. ECF No. 51-3

Her lawyers send him a formal written notice to preserve everything that might be relevant to the case. The letter directed him to “preserve, maintain, prevent spoliation of, and not destroy” anything related to the matter. From this date at the latest, he had a legal duty to keep all evidence. She argues the duty started earlier, at the November leak. ECF No. 21-3

He later says on a livestream that he “ran like a whole redact” of his Discord during this time. He said it on a stream, not in court, but it became central to the spoliation motion more than a year later. He said it on a stream in May 2026, and the sanctions motion quoted it back at him. He also testified that he deleted his messages with one witness “sometime maybe at the end of 2024,” and that he had saved copies with Redact, an app for deleting messages in bulk, and handed those copies over. His position is that removing material from view is not the same as destroying it. Peters Decl. ¶¶ 38–39, ECF No. 263 · Dep. Tr. 243:25–244:10
Filed February 18, 2025. From here on, almost everything is on the docket.

She brings four separate claims against him, all four about sharing the video. Only one comes from a federal law, and it’s the reason a federal court can hear the case. The complaint numbers them Counts I to IV. 15 U.S.C. § 6851. A federal law from 2022 that lets people sue someone who shares their intimate images without consent. Florida Statute § 784.049. Florida’s sexual cyberharassment law, which also lets victims sue. Intentional infliction of emotional distress. A claim Florida courts recognize on their own; it isn’t in any statute. Invasion of privacy (the complaint calls it “public disclosure of private facts”). Also a claim built up by the courts rather than written in a statute. The three Florida claims couldn’t have brought the case to federal court by themselves. A federal court can hear a case that’s only about state law when the two sides live in different states, and she and Bonnell both lived in Florida when she filed. The Florida claims are allowed in because they grew out of the same facts as the federal one. ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 3–7, 39–68 · 15 U.S.C. § 6851 · Fla. Stat. § 784.049

The court granted it the day after it was filed, and he did not object. The order keeps any filing that identifies her under seal, lets his lawyers have her real name if they ask, and forbids giving it to the media unless her lawyers agree. The federal law itself allows people suing under it to use a stand-in name. ECF No. 7 · 15 U.S.C. § 6851(b)(3)(B)
Motion for a restraining order and injunction

She asks for four forms of relief, five months after the leak. The plaintiff asked the court to order the defendant to stop sharing the video, take down the copies he controlled, and tell third parties in writing to remove their own. The fourth request was to preserve evidence. The first three all aimed at publication that had already happened, which is most of why the motion failed. ECF No. 21 at 6

The judge finds no emergency. Her own lawyer admits that “most of the damage has already been done.” Judge Becerra: “There is nothing that’s happening today that wasn’t happening when you filed the suit.” The court also told counsel that spoliation relief needs its own separately filed motion under Rule 37(e), advice not acted on for another thirteen months. ECF No. 38 at 5:19–23, 6:3
He opposes the injunction and files the date screenshots

He files screenshots of the same chat taken from both ends. His end reads 4/9/2022, and the recipient’s end reads 10/04/2022. This is the exhibit that settled when he first sent the video. It shows the same exchange captured from both ends of the conversation. A later message in the same chat is stamped 14/04/2022, and since there is no fourteenth month, the dates have to be day first. ECF Nos. 42, 42-4

Abbymc swears that he sent her the video in November 2023. It is the main evidence for one of the two ways the federal claim can survive. It’s two pages long and sworn under penalty of perjury. It says he sent her the video and that she recognized the plaintiff in it, but it attaches no message, no link and no file to back that up. That gap becomes the defendant’s main objection when he asks for summary judgment. ECF No. 49-2
Motion for a protective order over discovery

Filed after the negotiation between counsel breaks down. Before filing a motion like this, the lawyers have to talk it through, which courts call meeting and conferring. The court later found that her side declared those talks “exhausted” about thirty-six hours after sending an eleven-page draft, and two minutes before his lawyer replied that he had already marked it up. ECF Nos. 82, 92-3

Both parties testify for about two and a half hours, in open court. She testified that she had never personally seen any proof that he sent the video to anyone after October 2022. He testified that he never got her consent to share it, spoken or written, but believed their earlier messages implied it. ECF No. 90 at 55:7–13, 83:7–13

The court writes its own version, closer to the draft the two sides had worked out together. It covers intimate images, her legal name, the names of sealed non-party witnesses, and medical records, and it bars disclosure of any of it to the media or to “any online broadcast, podcast, stream, post or direct message.” ECF No. 116 ¶¶ 2, 7
Leave to amend granted: She is allowed to rewrite her complaint

The court calls the evidence of the timeline “murky at best.” It noted that the defendant’s own exhibit contains a screenshot taken from the recipient’s side of the chat, an image he could not have captured himself, and that no testimony from that recipient was ever offered to explain it. ECF No. 119 at 8

It keeps the same four claims and adds the Abbymc transmission and the continuing-accessibility theory. Both are attempts to show something he did after the law took effect that the law covers. The court had just ruled that the changes would not be futile, meaning they had at least some chance of working, which is a low bar but not nothing. ECF No. 120 ¶¶ 13–15, 45

On a livestream he describes reconstructing a log. Days later he files a log with the court. Whether it is the same one is disputed. On the stream he said, “There is no original file. I’m trying to reconstruct the file. I’m artificially creating a file by reconstructing a log of stuff.” On September 19 he filed a log and swore it was a true and correct record of everything he had sent Abbymc. The plaintiff says that is the file he was describing. At his deposition he said he did not remember which file the stream was about, that the filed log was a filtered list of his own sent messages, and that the merging only lined up timestamps and changed no message. Her filings date the clip to September 8 in one place and September 9 in another. ECF Nos. 139 at 13, 150 (audio), 132-6 · Dep. Tr. 311:4–313:20 (the clip, as played), 305:8–307:19, 314:5–318:9

He argues no jurisdiction: the only transmission of the video was before the law took effect. It challenges the facts behind jurisdiction, under Rule 12(b)(1). A motion like that lets the judge look at evidence beyond what the complaint and answer say, instead of assuming the complaint is true, and it puts the burden on the plaintiff to show the court has the power to hear the case. If the federal claim goes, he asks the judge to dismiss the three Florida claims too, since Florida courts should decide Florida law. He asks for that without prejudice, which means she could bring those claims again in a Florida court. ECF No. 132

She asserts in a footnote that the person he sent the video to was a minor. That claim becomes the Rule 11 fight. The claim rested on a redacted driving record that was supposed to show the recipient’s date of birth. It fell apart three weeks later at the Illinois deposition, when the woman whose identity was used testified that a man had been running the account. What the Rule 11 motion really goes after is not the footnote itself but her side’s refusal to file a correction afterward. ECF Nos. 139 at 7 n.2, 139-2

The court also notes that no spoliation motion has been filed. The court found no harm that money could not make up for later. She had waited five months without a convincing reason, and her own post saying she wanted him to “lose so much money” showed that money could cover the harm. The request about the forum failed because the rule for these orders, Rule 65, only binds the people in the case and those acting with them, and the forum is neither. ECF Nos. 143 at 12, 142

The woman whose identity the “Rose” account used testifies that she never spoke to him, and that an adult man in the United Kingdom was pretending to be her. She testified she never messaged him, never saw the video, and had no idea who the plaintiff was. She also explained why the leaked screenshots carry European date formatting, the single most useful fact the defense obtained in discovery. Brettler Decl. Ex. L at 67:13–24, 79:22–80:7

The hearing was public and the material was already in her own filings. No one had asked to close the courtroom, and people outside the case were there. The passages she wanted sealed, including the ones about suicidal thoughts, had been in her own complaint on the public docket since February. Because they were already public, the request failed. ECF No. 154 at 6–10
The plaintiff misses her own deposition

She had not asked the court to excuse her, and because she did not show, both her deposition and his get pushed back. Defense counsel had traveled for it. No relief was requested and no explanation filed. The court issued an order to show cause two days later and stayed the defendant’s deposition until the dispute was resolved. ECF Nos. 163, 167

The court also orders the plaintiff to explain why she missed hers. Later, she points to this stay to explain why her spoliation motion came so late. She argues that her proof he got rid of things on purpose could only come from his own testimony, and she could not get that until the court lifted the stay the following April. ECF No. 167 · ECF No. 275 at 2

A month before the cutoff. She produces nothing, and he never moves to compel. Served three and a half weeks before the discovery cutoff, after six months of disputed attempts. When she produced nothing he pursued neither a motion to compel under Rule 45(d)(2)(B)(i) nor contempt under Rule 45(g), and opposed the extension that would have allowed more time. ECF No. 212-10

Over the minor allegation in the footnote. Safe harbor observed and errata demanded first. His strongest point is relevance: whether the recipient was seventeen has no bearing on whether the transmission preceded October 1, 2022, which is the only thing his own motion is about. The court denied the motion without prejudice on April 21, 2026. ECF No. 183 · ECF No. 240

The sanctions motion is itself sanctionable. It rests on the Advisory Committee’s own note that a sanctions motion is subject to the rule, and on decisions from this district, one written by this magistrate judge, holding that Rule 11 is not a vehicle for resolving a disputed fact. It was denied without prejudice in the same order as his. ECF No. 186 · ECF No. 240

With the production disputes unresolved and no motion to compel ever filed. Neither side filed one. That single fact shapes everything after it: his complaint about an untested witness and her complaint about an incomplete production both arrive without the remedy that was available to fix them. ECF No. 23

The same jurisdictional argument, now on the full discovery record. Under Rule 56 he may carry his initial burden simply by pointing to an absence of evidence. He went further and filed affirmative evidence too, including his log of the media files he had sent the witness. The plaintiff says it is the log he described reconstructing on stream four months earlier. ECF Nos. 210, 213-5

Asking the court to defer for discovery not yet taken. It asked the court to deny or defer until his deposition and a Swedish deposition could be taken. It was the third time in four months she had asked the court to wait for discovery, and the court had already remarked on the pattern. ECF No. 216

Did he share it without her consent?

Plaintiff Yes, and he has admitted it. She authorized no one. Her account is that she agreed he could show it to his then-fiancée and was explicit that it go no further. Defendant He does not deny the transmission. He argues the surrounding exchanges implied permission, and that he never identified her by name to the recipient. Court No merits ruling. He testified he obtained neither verbal nor written consent. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Plaintiff The argument The statute does not recognize silence or atmosphere as consent. It defines it as an affirmative, conscious, and voluntary authorization. Nothing of that kind exists anywhere in the record, and he does not claim it does. Rests on His own sworn declaration admitting the transmission; his hearing testimony that he never obtained verbal or written consent; his message to her on the day of the leak, apologizing and saying there was no excuse; her declaration that she permitted his then-fiancée and no one else. ECF Nos. 42-1, 90, 120 Authority 15 U.S.C. § 6851(a)(2) supplies the definition of consent. Where it is weak None of consequence. This is the strongest element of her case, and the defense does not seriously contest it. Defendant The argument He is not arguing that she said yes. He is arguing that two people who had spent a year exchanging explicit material of themselves and their partners had established a shared understanding, and that he acted inside it, anonymously, without ever naming her. Rests on Their 2020 message history, filed as exhibits; his testimony that he believed he had implied consent given the norms of his circles; the fact that she raised no objection to his then-fiancée viewing it. ECF Nos. 42-3, 50-2, 90 Authority None directly. No authority is cited for implied consent under this statute, because the statute runs the other way. Where it is weak Fatal on this element. § 6851(b)(2)(A) says in terms that consenting to the recording is not consenting to its distribution. A court has already rejected a materially identical argument as contrary to the statute's plain language. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Did she give affirmative, conscious, voluntary authorization to share it? Defendant He concedes he never asked her. Statutory bar § 6851(b)(2)(A): consent to creation is not consent to distribution. Defense route The context of their exchanges implied permission. Plaintiff The implied-consent route is closed by the text of the statute itself. Where it lands Element satisfied, but only if the statute reaches the conduct at all. That question is Dispute 7.

Plaintiff Pleaded October 2022, then “sometime in 2022,” and in May 2026 conceded April 9, 2022, before the statute. Her own expert reached that date first. Defendant April 9, 2022. The screenshot reading 10/04/22 is the recipient’s side of the chat in day/month format, because the account was run from the United Kingdom. Court Called the timeline “murky at best” in September 2025. The concession came eight months later. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Plaintiff The argument Her original reading was not unreasonable on the face of the document, and her objection was never really about arithmetic. It was about provenance: the exhibit he relies on contains a screenshot taken from the recipient's side of the conversation. He could not have produced that image from his own account, and the person who supposedly took it never testified. Rests on The ambiguity of 10/04/22 standing alone; the unexplained origin of the recipient-side image; the absence of that recipient as a witness for the defense. ECF No. 119 Authority No presumption of truth attaches to either side on a factual jurisdictional attack, so the evidence has to actually establish the date. Where it is weak She lost this one. Her own forensic expert accepted April 2022 in October 2025 and she conceded formally in May 2026. Whatever the provenance question, this route to a federal claim is now closed by her own admission. Defendant The argument The date is not a matter of interpretation once you put the two sides of the same conversation next to each other. His side reads 4/9/2022 at 8:28 PM. The recipient's side reads 10/04/2022 at 1:28 am: the same messages, four hours and thirty-eight minutes apart, which is exactly Miami to London. Rests on The paired screenshots of the identical exchange; a control message stamped 14/04/2022 , which can only be read day-first because there is no fourteenth month; the deposition of the woman whose identity was borrowed, who confirmed the account was run by a man living in the United Kingdom; and the leaker's own published post, in which every date appears in European format. ECF Nos. 42-4, 132-3 Authority Landgraf v. USI Film Products bars retroactive effect without clear congressional intent. Three district courts have applied that to this statute specifically. Where it is weak He raised jurisdiction in responses for roughly six months before filing an actual motion, which the court noted. And the provenance point the plaintiff raised was never answered: he has still not explained how he came to hold an image taken from the other side of the chat. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test The screenshot reads 10/04/22 . Is that October 4 or April 10? If October 4, 2022 After the statute. The federal claim stands on this transmission alone. If April 10, 2022 Before the statute. This route is closed. Defendant Control test: a later message in the same thread is stamped 14/04/2022 . There is no fourteenth month, so the format is day-first. Defendant Corroboration: the account holder's deposition places the correspondent in the United Kingdom. Plaintiff Unanswered: the exhibit includes an image from the recipient's side that he could not have captured himself, and that recipient never testified. Where it lands Resolved in the defendant's favor. The plaintiff conceded April 9, 2022, in May 2026. Jurisdiction must now come from somewhere else.
Was there a second transmission, after the statute?

Plaintiff Yes. November 2023, to “Abbymc,” supported by two sworn declarations and a message that witness sent a friend the same morning. Defendant It never happened. His preserved logs list every file he sent her and the video is not among them. The witness never testified, produced nothing under subpoena, and later distanced herself. Court Undecided. This is the question summary judgment turns on. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Plaintiff The argument The strongest piece is a clock. The witness's message to a friend is timestamped 10:41 in the morning. The two links the defendant says account for that day are logged at 2:39 in the afternoon. A message sent at 10:41 cannot be describing something that arrived four hours later. Something else came that morning. Rests on Two sworn declarations from the witness; the screenshot of her 10:41 message; the defendant's own log, which puts his links at 2:39 p.m.; his admission that he deleted his messages with her from Discord, which is where the direct proof would have been. ECF Nos. 49-2, 86-1, 249-1 · Dep. Tr. 243:25–244:10 Authority Rule 56(c)(2) requires only that evidence be reducible to admissible form at trial: it has to be capable of being put in proper form later, not already in that form now. Rule 901's authentication bar is low, and the author has twice sworn the message is hers. Where it is weak Serious. The witness never sat for deposition, produced nothing under a validly served subpoena, and days after signing her first declaration told the defendant she no longer wanted to be involved. A second declaration appeared after discovery had closed and after the plaintiff testified she had no recent contact with her. The clock is also less fixed than it looks. At deposition he agreed the log reads 2:39 p.m. but said he could not tell whether that was Eastern or universal time. In universal time it would be 10:39 a.m. in Miami, two minutes before her message. Dep. Tr. 221:3–13 Defendant The argument The plaintiff's entire federal case rests on one witness who has never been tested and one message that does not say what she needs it to say. It names no sender, attaches no video, produces no link, and is offered for the truth of what it asserts. Rests on His preserved communication log, which he swore identified every media file he ever sent her and in which the video's filename does not appear; the two Drive links from that day, which he says held videos of another woman who confirmed as much; proof of service of the subpoena she ignored. ECF Nos. 132-6, 213-5 Authority Anderson v. Liberty Lobby requires the side opposing summary judgment to produce evidence that is significantly probative, not merely colorable: enough for a jury to act on, not just enough to sound plausible. Cases from this district exclude affidavits where the opponent was denied a meaningful chance to test the witness. Where it is weak Two problems. He served that subpoena a month before the cutoff and then never moved to compel or for contempt, while opposing the extension that would have allowed more pursuit, so the gap he complains of is partly his own. And his opposition to the sanctions motion concedes the log he calls complete is not. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Is there evidence of a disclosure after October 1, 2022? Plaintiff The witness swears she received the video on or about November 3, 2023, and messaged a friend about it that morning at 10:41 a.m. Defendant The only things sent that day were two links to another woman's videos, logged at 2:39 p.m. Plaintiff A 10:41 message cannot describe a 2:39 event. Something arrived earlier. The reply brief does not answer this. Defendant But the witness was never deposed, produced nothing under subpoena, and later disavowed involvement. If a jury could believe her Genuine dispute of material fact. Summary judgment denied and the case goes to trial. If the declaration is not probative No post-statute transmission is established. Judgment for the defendant. Where it lands Undecided. The single most consequential open question in the case.
Does leaving a file reachable count as sharing it?

Plaintiff The statute defines “disclose” to include make accessible, a continuing state, not a single moment. He controlled the file and left it reachable until he deleted it in November 2024. Defendant A private link sent to one person is not publication. Courts have held that an unguessable, unindexed link is not public access, and no court has stretched the statute this way. Court Undecided, but treated as serious enough to allow the amendment that raised it. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Plaintiff The argument This is the argument that could win the case even after losing the date. Congress wrote four verbs: transfer, publish, distribute, or make accessible. If the fourth meant only the instant of sending, it would do no work the first three do not already do. Reading it as a continuing condition gives it meaning, and on that reading the defendant kept the video accessible for twenty-five months after the statute took effect. Rests on The statutory text; her expert's analysis of how the platform stores and serves attachments; and above all the defendant's own deposition admission that the file remained reachable on his account or the recipient's until he deleted it in November 2024. ECF No. 139-1 · Dep. Tr. 199:15–200:11 Authority 15 U.S.C. § 6851(a)(4). A district court has held that continued post-enactment availability is itself a disclosure, regardless of when the material first went up. Where it is weak Her own expert conceded the link was effectively unguessable and that it is not known whether search engines ever indexed it. That guts the public accessibility half of the theory. What is left is the narrower version, that he simply failed to delete it, which is not quite what the amended complaint pleads. Defendant The argument Sending one person a private link is not publishing. The plaintiff is trying to convert a single message into a continuing act so that conduct from April 2022 can be prosecuted under a statute passed six months later, which is retroactivity by another name. Rests on Two Arizona decisions holding that a long, non-guessable, unindexed URL is not public access, and that emailing such a link to one person is nothing like publishing in a newspaper. The plaintiff's lead authority involved posting to a public pornography site. Authority Wray v. Greenburg and Greenburg v. Wray; Landgraf on retroactivity. Where it is weak His factual premise is shakier than the brief admits. He told the court the video went only as a platform attachment and not by Drive link, but the leaker's own published post shows Drive links were in fact sent to that recipient. He also declined to engage this theory at all in his summary judgment motion and addressed it only on reply. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Does make accessible describe a continuing state, or only the moment of sending? If a continuing state Then ask the next question: was it still accessible after October 1, 2022? If only the moment Only April 2022 counts. This route closes and everything rides on Dispute 3. Defendant He admits he did not delete it until November 2024, so on his own account, yes. Defendant But accessible to whom? Her expert concedes the link was unguessable and may never have been indexed. Plaintiff The statute says make accessible, not publish. It does not obviously require the public. Where it lands An open question of first impression. If it resolves for the plaintiff, jurisdiction survives even if Dispute 3 fails.
Does her earlier conduct amount to consent?

Plaintiff The statute forecloses the argument in terms: agreeing to be recorded is not agreeing to distribution, and having shared something once is not agreement to share it again. Defendant He has not moved for judgment on consent. He offers the history for credibility and damages, pointing to a public statement of hers he says his own exhibits contradict. Court Not ruled. Both sides have asked to exclude the other’s material at trial. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Plaintiff The argument Congress anticipated this defense and wrote it out of the statute in two sentences. Beyond that, the material is exactly what the rules of evidence keep out of a civil trial: sexual history offered to make a jury think less of the person it happened to. Rests on The statutory text; a decision rejecting an identical argument; and the defendant's own testimony that he never asked her. ECF No. 90 Authority 15 U.S.C. § 6851(b)(2)(A) and (B); Aaron v. Ferrell; Federal Rules of Evidence 412 and 403. Where it is weak One exhibit her own side filed is a message in which she tells him he had been very clear about how seriously he takes consent, which the defense can use on the reasonableness of his belief, even if belief is not a defense. Defendant The argument He is not asking a jury to find she consented. He is asking that a jury be allowed to hear that she publicly said she had never sent him videos of other people, when his exhibits show she did, because a case that turns on whose account to believe cannot be tried with one side's credibility sealed off. Rests on The 2020 message history; her January 2025 public statement; her deposition testimony. ECF Nos. 42-3, 50-1 Authority Rule 412's own exceptions and Rule 403 balancing, which he argues permit the material for impeachment rather than consent. Where it is weak The line is not as clean as the brief makes it. Roughly seven pages of a purely jurisdictional summary judgment motion are given over to her sexual history, none of which bears on the October 2022 date. The plaintiff declined to answer it on the merits and preserved her objection, which is a strong position to be in. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Is the history relevant to consent? Plaintiff No. § 6851(b)(2)(A) and (B) exclude it by statute: creation is not distribution, and one disclosure is not permission for the next. Test Is it relevant to credibility instead? Plaintiff Even so, Rule 412 applies, and its balance is reversed: probative value must substantially outweigh the harm. Defendant Yes. She made a public statement his own exhibits contradict. Where it lands Turns on the motions in limine. Either way it cannot establish the defense, and at most it touches weight and damages.

Plaintiff He deleted his side of conversations with several women after a preservation letter, and swore to a “true and correct” log of everything he sent one of them that omits two links his own production shows him sending. Defendant Nothing was lost. Removing material from public view at her request is not destruction, the omission was inadvertent, and the motion arrived five months after discovery closed, a discovery complaint relabeled as spoliation. Court Argued August 19, 2026, with evidence heard on October 2. Undecided, and now first in line. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Plaintiff The argument The centrepiece is a document he filed himself. He swore that a spreadsheet was a true and correct log of every media file and link he ever sent that witness. His own produced chat thread shows two links that are not on it, one of them introduced by a message asking whether he had already sent her a particular video. Either that link showed the plaintiff, which proves the transmission he denies, or his sworn statement of completeness is false. There is no third option. Rests on The conceded omission; his deposition testimony that the underlying files no longer exist; a public statement that he ran a wholesale redaction of his messages in early 2025; three productions about the same witness that disagree with each other, one carrying a different username; and the fact that he produced the attachments she sent him and none that he sent her. ECF Nos. 263, 272 · Dep. Tr. 237:3–6 Authority Rule 37(e)(2), which allows an adverse inference or judgment where a party acted with intent to deprive. Where it is weak The timing is close to indefensible. The court noted in October 2025 that no spoliation motion was on file. The motion deadline passed in March 2026. She filed in May. Edwin Torres, the magistrate judge on this case, has turned down motions like this as too late in his own earlier opinions, and the defense cites two of them. Defendant The argument This is a discovery dispute that was never brought, arriving as a sanctions motion after the deadline for both. Rule 37(e)(2) requires bad faith, not untidiness, and the two links she calls missing were produced to her eight months before she filed. Rests on The production history; his testimony that he preserved and produced everything in his possession; the court's own observation, early in the case, that someone removing intimate material after being sued is not necessarily spoliating; and her own request that he take the material down, the one exhibit he put in at the October hearing. ECF Nos. 272, 272-1 · Dep. Tr. 366:12–367:6, 369:21–370:7 Authority Skanska and Tesoriero hold that intent to deprive means bad faith, and that negligence is not enough. A line of decisions from this district denying spoliation motions filed after the discovery cutoff. Where it is weak The substance is where he is most exposed anywhere in the case. He generated no hash values, produced 2,400 pages as a flat PDF with no metadata, publicly described artificially reconstructing a log, refused a cost-shared neutral forensic examination and then argued she never conducted one, and he conceded the sworn log is incomplete. On hash values his answer at deposition was that they would be meaningless when the chain of custody starts with him. Dep. Tr. 297:16–299:10 Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Is the motion timely? Defendant Discovery closed December 2025. The motion deadline was March 2026. She filed in May 2026. Plaintiff The intent evidence came from his April 2026 deposition, which the court itself had stayed. She filed eighteen days later. If timely The Rule 37(e) elements are reached and the merits below are decided. If untimely Denied without reaching the merits at all. This is the live risk for the plaintiff. Test Was there a duty to preserve, was information lost, and was it lost with intent to deprive? Plaintiff Duty attached by the January 2025 letter at the latest. He testified the files no longer exist. He swore to a complete log that his own opposition concedes is not complete. Defendant Inadvertent. The links were produced. Removal from public view was at her own request. Where it lands If intent is found, sanctions run from an adverse-inference instruction up to judgment on liability, which would end the merits of the case in her favor.
Should a federal court hear this at all?

Plaintiff Yes. The November 2023 transmission and the continuing accessibility of the file both land after the statute took effect, and either is enough. If the federal claim fails anyway, the judge should still keep her three Florida claims. Defendant No. The only established transmission predates the statute by nearly six months. Without the federal claim, her three Florida claims should be dismissed with it. Court Warned in October 2025 that jurisdiction may be absent. Still undecided, and stayed since September 2026 until the spoliation ruling. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Plaintiff The argument She accepts the burden. She needs one qualifying disclosure after October 1, 2022, and she has pleaded two independent routes to one.
